structures.title: Basic statement word order
structures.explanation: Portuguese default order is subject-verb-object, like English. Because verb endings show the person, the subject pronoun is often dropped when clear. Adjectives, however, usually follow the noun they describe.

structures.title: Forming yes/no questions
structures.explanation: The most common way to ask a yes/no question is to keep statement order and raise your intonation at the end. Inversion (verb before subject) is possible but formal. No auxiliary 'do' is needed.
structures.ex2_ref: Is everything all right with you?

structures.title: Negating and double negatives
structures.explanation: Place não directly before the verb to negate. Portuguese uses double negatives: when a negative word like nada, ninguém, or nunca follows the verb, não stays before it. This is required, not an error.
structures.ex2_ref: I didn't see anyone at the party.

structures.title: Expressing the near future
structures.explanation: Conjugate ir in the present and add the main verb's infinitive to talk about plans and things about to happen. It is the everyday future in Brazil. Do not insert any preposition between the two verbs.
structures.ex2_ref: They're going to travel in the summer.

structures.title: Present progressive (Brazil)
structures.explanation: Combine estar (conjugated) with the gerund (verb minus -r plus -ndo) for an action happening right now. The gerund never changes for gender or number. This is the standard Brazilian form.

structures.title: Saying what you like
structures.explanation: Gostar always takes the preposition de before what you like. De contracts with articles: de+o=do, de+a=da. Follow it with a noun or an infinitive verb.

structures.title: Expressing obligation
structures.explanation: Use ter que (or ter de) plus an infinitive to say you have to do something. Ter que is more common in speech. Precisar de + noun or precisar + infinitive expresses need similarly.
structures.ex1_target: Tenho que estudar para a prova.
structures.ex1_ref: I have to study for the test.

structures.title: Real (first) conditional
structures.explanation: For a likely future condition, use se plus the future subjunctive, then a present or future main clause. English uses the present here, but Portuguese needs the future subjunctive after se.
structures.ex1_target: Se eu tiver tempo, vou à academia.
structures.ex1_ref: If I have time, I'll go to the gym.
structures.ex2_target: Se você quiser, a gente sai mais cedo.
structures.ex2_ref: If you want, we'll leave earlier.

structures.title: Making comparisons
structures.explanation: Put mais (more) or menos (less) before the adjective and (do) que after it to compare two things. The do is optional but common. For equality use tão + adjective + quanto.
structures.ex1_target: Ela é mais alta do que eu.
structures.ex1_ref: She is taller than I am.
structures.ex2_target: Este livro é menos caro que aquele.
structures.ex2_ref: This book is less expensive than that one.

structures.title: Relative clause with que
structures.explanation: Que links a noun to a clause that describes it, working for both people and things ('who,' 'that,' 'which'). Unlike English, que can never be dropped in Portuguese.
structures.ex1_target: O homem que mora aqui é médico.
structures.ex1_ref: The man who lives here is a doctor.
structures.ex2_target: O filme que vimos foi ótimo.
structures.ex2_ref: The movie that we saw was great.

structures.title: Wanting someone else to act
structures.explanation: When you want another person to do something, use querer que plus the present subjunctive (not the infinitive). The change of subject across que triggers the subjunctive mood.
structures.ex1_target: Quero que você venha à minha festa.
structures.ex1_ref: I want you to come to my party.
structures.ex2_target: Ela quer que nós façamos o trabalho.
structures.ex2_ref: She wants us to do the work.

structures.title: Expressing purpose ('in order to')
structures.explanation: Use para plus an infinitive to state the purpose of an action ('in order to,' 'so as to'). If the second action has a different subject, use the personal infinitive after para.
structures.ex1_target: Estudo português para trabalhar no Brasil.
structures.ex1_ref: I study Portuguese in order to work in Brazil.
structures.ex2_target: Ele ligou para avisar do atraso.
structures.ex2_ref: He called to warn about the delay.

structures.title: Passive voice
structures.explanation: Form the passive with ser plus a past participle that agrees in gender and number with the subject. The agent, if named, follows por. It shifts focus from the doer to the thing affected.
structures.ex2_target: As casas foram construídas pela empresa.
structures.ex2_ref: The houses were built by the company.

structures.title: Reported (indirect) speech
structures.explanation: Report what someone said with a verb like dizer or falar plus que and a clause. When the main verb is past, the reported verb usually shifts to a past tense (present → imperfeito).
structures.ex2_target: Ela falou que vai chegar tarde.
structures.ex2_ref: She said she's going to arrive late.

structures.title: The superlative (the most … of)
structures.explanation: To say something is the most/least within a group, use the definite article plus mais/menos, the adjective, and de for the group. The article agrees with the noun in gender and number.
structures.ex1_target: Ela é a mais alta da turma.
structures.ex1_ref: She is the tallest in the class.
structures.ex2_target: É o restaurante mais famoso da cidade.
structures.ex2_ref: It's the most famous restaurant in the city.

structures.title: Concession ('although / even though')
structures.explanation: Embora ('although') always requires the subjunctive in the clause it introduces. It sets up a contrast with the main clause. Mesmo que and ainda que work the same way.
structures.ex1_ref: Although it's raining, I'm going to go out.
structures.ex2_target: Embora seja caro, vale a pena.
structures.ex2_ref: Even though it's expensive, it's worth it.
